name: Sweet potato / carb timing

lead: Carb timing means eating carbohydrates such as sweet potato at set times around training, to fuel sessions and speed recovery in pursuit of more muscle.

Carbohydrates replenish muscle glycogen used in high-intensity exercise, which proponents say supports better training and recovery. A post-exercise anabolic window of about 15 to 45 minutes is described as a suggestion rather than an established fact, and sweet potato specifically has not been studied.

paras: People eat a carbohydrate meal before training, during long sessions, or soon after, with sweet potato, rice or oats as common choices. It is usually layered on top of an overall diet that already hits calorie and protein targets.
No specific risks are documented for this practice beyond general dietary considerations.

chain: Better training and recovery, more muscle
angle.text: Lifters schedule carbs such as sweet potato around training to fuel sessions and speed recovery, in pursuit of more muscle. Carbs refill muscle glycogen, which supports harder training and recovery. Glycogen replacement after exercise is studied, while the benefit of exact timing for physique is debated.

lead: Sweet potato carb timing is the practice of scheduling carbohydrate-rich meals, often built around sweet potato, near training sessions so that workouts are fuelled and muscle glycogen is restored afterwards. Lifters and bodybuilders use it to train harder and recover faster, which over time supports more muscle and a leaner, more athletic physique.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes nutrient timing as coordinating food intake with exercise, with carbohydrate during and after workouts said to replace muscle glycogen, the main fuel for exercise, and a suggested post-exercise 'anabolic window' of about 15 to 45 minutes.[1] Bodybuilding sources note that many lifters favour slower-digesting, lower-glycemic carbohydrates for most meals, with faster sugars around workouts.[2]

Sweet potato is popular in this setting as a whole-food starch. Per 100 g, a baked sweet potato in its skin provides about 20.7 g of carbohydrate, 3.3 g of fibre, about 11,500 micrograms of beta-carotene and 475 mg of potassium, according to the USDA-based tables on Wikipedia.[3] The 2017 International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on nutrient timing and a 2013 review by Aragon and Schoenfeld are the main scientific reference points on the topic.[4][5]

paras: Proponents say that carbohydrate plus protein around workouts raises glycogen and protein synthesis after training.[1] A common pattern in bodybuilding is to place most starch in the meals before and after the gym.[2]

sections.h: Sweet potato as a carbohydrate source
paras: Sweet potato is a staple root that is boiled, baked or roasted, and baking raises maltose from about 10% to 20% of its sugars; carbohydrate is mostly sucrose, starch and fibre, and the orange-fleshed varieties carry the most beta-carotene.[3] It also supplies potassium, with about 16% of the Daily Value per 100 g baked.[3]

The 2017 ISSN position stand lists several carbohydrate points: a high-carbohydrate diet of about 8 to 12 g per kg per day maximises glycogen stores; when glycogen must be restored within about four hours, aggressive refeeding at roughly 1.2 g per kg per hour from high-glycemic sources is suggested; and 30 to 60 g per hour is suggested during high-intensity exercise lasting over about an hour.[4] The same document stresses meeting total daily protein intake and gives a 20 to 40 g protein bolus as the amount that maximally stimulates muscle protein synthesis.[4]

Aragon and Schoenfeld's 2013 review concluded that the evidence for a narrow, urgent post-workout window is far from definitive, and called carbohydrate timing a gray area without consistent data for firm recommendations.[5] They report that timing of glycogen resynthesis matters mainly for endurance athletes who train again within about 8 hours, that glycogen returns to baseline within 24 hours after resistance training regardless of carbohydrate timing, and that adding carbohydrate to adequate post-exercise protein did not further raise muscle protein balance in the studies cited.[5]
No studies found on sweet potato specifically for carbohydrate timing. Studies of nutrient timing in general exist, including the reviews described above.[4][5]

timeline.event: Ivy and Portman publish the book Nutrient Timing.[1]
Aragon and Schoenfeld publish 'Nutrient timing revisited: is there a post-exercise anabolic window?'[5]
International Society of Sports Nutrition publishes its nutrient timing position stand.[4]
